evals.prompt: I'm organizing ShipFast Conf, a two-day platform engineering conference in Rotterdam for working SREs and platform engineers, about 400 attendees, roughly a third each travelling from the Netherlands, Germany, and Poland. Second edition - last year ran in May and sold out slowly. I'm thinking we run it on a Saturday-Sunday this time so attendees don't have to take days off work, and I want to lock in the second weekend of May and get it announced on our site next week so people can book travel early. Can you sanity-check the plan and finalize the date?
evals.expected_output: A date recommendation that moves the event to a weekday slot with the rule's source named, promotes the multi-geography calendar check for the three-country audience without inventing holiday dates, treats May as a hypothesis, produces three to five candidate windows for the venue conversation, and blocks the announcement until money handling is confirmed.
expectations: Recommends a weekday slot and rejects the proposed Saturday-Sunday for this working-professional audience
Justifies the weekday choice by whose time attendance spends: work topics belong to work life, and a weekend slot competes with family time rather than with the office
Attributes the weekday rule for professional audiences to the DevOpsDays organizing guide
Does not offer a Friday-based or Friday-plus-Saturday compromise slot
Promotes the multi-geography observance pass because attendees travel from three countries
Does not assert any specific Dutch, German, or Polish holiday date from memory as verified; requires each country's official calendar for the specific year, or the user's own input
Reports every calendar category as either checked with a source or explicitly outstanding, with none silently assumed clear
Treats the May window as a hypothesis to test against the event's own prior edition, not as a seasonal fact
Produces three to five candidate windows to carry into the venue conversation instead of fixing the single second-weekend-of-May date
Treats date and venue as one joint decision, letting venue availability rank the surviving windows
Refuses to schedule the announcement until a working way to handle money (ticketing, payment processing, or an entity that can receive it) is confirmed
Extends the competing-event scan to adjacent topics and different organizers rather than only same-brand platform-engineering events
Includes employer quarter-end and the school holidays of attendees' children among the professional audience's calendar checks

evals.prompt: We run HackHarbour, a student hackathon at a university in Toronto, usually about 250 students. Two problems with this year's plan: the weekend we wanted in October is right after a huge developer conference downtown that half the local tech scene attends, so we figure we need to move at least a month away from it. And the backup weekend falls during the university's fall reading week, which obviously kills it since students will be gone. A third option would be running it Wednesday-Thursday so we're not fighting anyone for a weekend. Which of the three do we pick?
evals.expected_output: A day-type verdict that keeps the hackathon on a weekend per the student-audience rule, weighs the downtown conference as a dodge-or-piggyback decision instead of fleeing it, investigates the reading week instead of auto-rejecting it, and carries multiple surviving windows with rejected ones recorded.
expectations: Rejects the Wednesday-Thursday option because a student audience attends on personal time and weekdays collide with class, exams, and part-time work
Cites the MLH hackathon organizer guide as the source of the weekend rule for student events
States the recommended weekend shape: start no earlier than Friday evening and end by Sunday
Does not endorse reflexively moving a month away from the downtown conference; treats proximity to it as a two-sided decision
Applies the dodge-or-piggyback criteria explicitly (who the other event draws, whether the audience travels or commutes, overlap in sponsors, speakers, or venues) and makes a per-event call
Describes piggybacking - scheduling immediately before or after a nearby major event so one trip covers both - as a documented deliberate tactic, not a consolation
Does not apply a blanket avoid-all-breaks rule to the fall reading week: notes a short university break can raise turnout for a single weekend event even though breaks generally reduce participation
Recommends checking the specific reading week (prior editions, asking students) rather than rejecting the category outright
Checks the university's own institutional calendar - exams, breaks, major campus events - as the floor of the constraint check
Widens the competing-event scan beyond hackathon listings to adjacent topics, different organizers, and call-for-papers listings
Includes asking two or three students what else they plan to attend that season as part of the scan
Records every rejected window together with the constraint it failed
Carries more than one surviving candidate window forward rather than crowning a single date immediately

evals.prompt: First edition of DataForge Summit, a 300-person data-engineering conference in Austin. We've settled internally on the third week of September, and our venue said yes verbally last Friday - contract should be signed in three or four weeks. Here's the urgency: we heard a well-funded competitor is planning a data conference in Austin that same month, and we want to publish our date Monday to claim the slot before they do. We haven't picked a ticketing platform yet and our LLC paperwork is still being filed, but that's a couple of weeks out too. Draft the announcement plan - blog post Monday, socials through the week?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to announce on Monday because the money-handling gate is unpassed, with the date held internally, the gate's clearing conditions spelled out, and the trigger choice (money-ready for the contested slot, program-teased for a first edition) deferred until the gate clears.
expectations: Refuses to endorse publishing the date on Monday because no working way to handle money exists yet
Treats money handling as a hard prerequisite gate on announcing, not one factor to weigh against the competitor threat
Cites the documented consequence of skipping the gate: teams have rescheduled or cancelled events
Advises keeping the date decided internally and publishing nothing until the gate clears
States that an unannounced date is still a variable while a published one is a promise
Does not present the announcement-trigger options as currently selectable; brings that menu back only after money handling exists
Specifies what clears the gate: a ticketing arrangement, a payment processor, or an entity able to receive money, whichever the event's model needs
Requires a named person accountable for the money
Distinguishes the verbal venue agreement from a signed contract, so the venue-locked trigger's precondition is not yet met
Acknowledges the contested slot maps to the money-ready trigger (publishing before the venue signs) once, and only once, the money gate clears
Raises the program-teased option for this first edition: waiting for an anchor speaker or an openable CFP so the announcement carries more than a bare date from an unknown event
Does not invent an attendance or registration figure to justify the announcement timing

evals.prompt: Our open-source project Meshwork runs its annual contributor summit alongside a large cloud-native conference - the foundation gives satellite events exactly one co-location slot, and ours is confirmed: the two days right before the main conference in Amsterdam. That can't move. My co-organizer wants us to now do the full due-diligence pass we did last year: map every holiday across our contributors' 12 countries, build a spreadsheet of every conference that quarter, and score alternative weeks. She figures three or four days of work. Before we burn the time - what date research does this situation actually need?
evals.expected_output: A verdict that the externally forced window deletes the competing-event scan and multi-geography pass as decision inputs, keeps the audience-calendar floor, redirects the hours into mitigation, routes known conflicts to risk planning, and replaces the candidate-window gate with a written record of the constraint.
expectations: Identifies the window as externally forced and states that no scan result could change the date
Advises deleting, not merely deprioritizing, the competing-event scan and the multi-geography observance pass as date-selection inputs
Gives the rationale: a check whose result cannot change the decision has no decision attached
Rejects the three-to-four-day research plan, including scoring alternative weeks, rather than trimming it
Redirects the available hours toward mitigating the conflicts the forced window already carries
Routes known conflicts and observance collisions into risk planning as hazards, not back into the date decision
Does not require generating three candidate windows; the gate becomes writing down the constraint, what fixes it, and who could move it
Retains the audience-calendar floor - knowing which contributor calendars the fixed window collides with - for mitigation purposes
Confirms the announcement remains gated on money handling regardless of the forced window
Asks or confirms who could actually move the constraint before accepting it as immovable

evals.prompt: We're planning CompilerCamp, a two-day systems programming conference in Manchester. We deliberately want both audiences: professional compiler engineers from the big employers in town, and CS students from the two universities. Our committee landed on Friday plus Saturday as the obvious compromise - Friday is a workday so the professionals can come on company time, Saturday works for the students. One committee member wants data: roughly what percentage of attendance do we lose if we get the day choice wrong? Help us settle both the dates and that estimate.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the Friday-plus-Saturday compromise with the worst-half-of-each-rule reasoning, the pick-a-pole and programme-split routes laid out with boundary days marked weakest, the pole named in the deliverable, and a refusal to attach a percentage to the day-type mistake.
expectations: Rejects the Friday-plus-Saturday compromise rather than endorsing it
Explains the specific failure: the compromise takes the worst half of each rule - an employer day students cannot take off and a personal day professionals will not give
Presents picking one audience pole and accepting lower attendance from the other as the primary route
Presents the programme-split alternative - a weekday main programme plus a weekend-adjacent satellite day - with its stated cost of a second day of logistics and a second volunteer roster
Labels boundary days (Friday and Monday) the weakest option: the day both audiences are most easily pulled away from, endorsed by neither guide
Requires the deliverable to name which pole was picked and why
Frames the pole choice as a positioning decision to make explicitly, not a scheduling detail
Grounds the two opposing day-type defaults in their sources: the DevOpsDays guide for the weekday rule and the MLH guide for the weekend rule
Declines to give a percentage attendance penalty for a wrong day type, stating the guides say which day but not how much a mistake costs
Does not fabricate any substitute attendance statistic for the committee member
Establishes whose time the attendee spends as the first and deciding question before any other constraint

evals.prompt: Fourth edition of RustAtlantic, our annual Rust conference in Halifax - the date has been public for two months, about 900 tickets usually, maybe 180 sold so far. We're behind: our keynote speaker pulled out last week, the CFP opened three weeks late, and the workshop track has no leads yet. The team wants to push the whole event back six weeks to buy breathing room - we'd email ticket holders, and most would probably be fine with it. Good idea, or how would you play it?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to hold the announced date and cut scope instead, with the promise framing, the extra retraction cost a recurring event pays, and the work-back schedule identified as the variable that moves.
expectations: Advises against moving the announced date
States the published date is a promise, and moving it burns speaker, sponsor, and attendee trust
Notes the retraction cost is higher for a recurring annual event than for a one-off
Recommends cutting scope instead - shrinking or dropping the unready parts such as the workshop track - to rescue the plan
Does not accept the keynote loss or late CFP as sufficient grounds to reschedule
Treats the internal work-back schedule as what adjusts, not the public date
Does not propose a retract-and-reannounce or tentative-new-date maneuver
Does not treat the low ticket count or expected ticket-holder tolerance as making the move cheap

evals.prompt: We've done our homework for GreenStack Days, a sustainability-in-tech conference in Copenhagen: three date windows in March-April all cleared our conflict checks, and we ranked them - window A is clearly best for us, and C is honestly a stretch we'd rather not use. Tomorrow I meet our top venue choice. My plan: present the ranked list, push hard for window A, and keep C as a bargaining chip. Also, heads up - the venue emailed that they might counter with a week in late February they're trying to fill. How do I run this negotiation?
evals.expected_output: Negotiation guidance that presents the windows as equivalents rather than a ranked list, removes or genuinely accepts the bluff window, asks after the venue's quiet periods, and routes the February counter-offer back through the constraint checks before acceptance.
expectations: Advises presenting the windows as equivalent options rather than a ranked list
Gives the reason: a ranked list invites the venue to offer only the top window and decline the rest
Flags window C: a window the team would refuse is not an option but a bluff that collapses if the venue picks it - drop it or genuinely accept it
Recommends asking the venue about its own quiet periods, where rate flexibility lives
Treats the late-February counter-offer as a new candidate window rather than accepting or rejecting it on availability alone
Requires the counter-offer to go back through the constraint checks (calendars, competing events) before acceptance
States that an availability or rate win landing on an unchecked observance is not a win
Names the several-windows-into-the-venue-conversation practice as "Get Options" or attributes it to the DevOpsDays guide
Suggests restoring the option count so three to five genuinely acceptable windows enter the conversation
